issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment that restores the prior statutory position and does not impair an acquired right is not invalid merely because it changes the compensation a claimant could otherwise have obtained.
material_facts: A later enactment operated retrospectively to remove amendments that had shifted the deemed date of vesting.
The respondent relied on those amendments to claim compensation calculated under the earlier, more favourable rate.
The Court found that the later enactment restored the position that had existed under the principal legislation and did not affect a vested or acquired right.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective enactment was not unconstitutional under Article 14 on the facts of this case.
issues.legal_principle: The legislature may amend, repeal, or omit legislation retrospectively, subject to constitutional limitations including Article 14. Retrospective legislation is not per se unconstitutional merely because it affects rights; the law must be assessed against the rights accrued at the time of review. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Raman Lal Keshav Lal Soni, T.R. Kapur v. State of Haryana, and Union of India v. Tushar Ranjan Mohanty.

rule.if: retrospective_legislation_challenge and retrospective_change_restores_prior_position and no_acquired_right_affected and no_other_article_14_violation_shown

predicates.retrospective_legislation_challenge: A party challenges the constitutionality of legislation that changes the law with retrospective effect.
predicates.retrospective_change_restores_prior_posi: The legislature’s retrospective change restores the position that existed before the intervening amendment.
predicates.no_acquired_right_affected: The retrospective change does not impair a vested or acquired right.
predicates.no_other_article_14_violation_shown: The challenger has not established another basis on which the retrospective change violates equality guarantees.

issues.definition: When a retrospective-legislation challenge concerns a change that restores the prior position, affects no acquired right, and shows no other equality violation, the rule treats the retrospective law as not invalid under Article 14.

issues.legal_issue: A later enactment that retrospectively deems an amendment never to have been made removes the basis of a judgment founded on that amendment, and the court must decide the pending appeal on the altered legal footing.
material_facts: The High Court directed compensation to be calculated by relying on a retrospective amendment that deemed vesting to have occurred earlier.
The later enactment expressly deemed that amendment never to have been made and addressed the effect of judgments and orders.
The appeals against the High Court judgments were still pending, and the judgments rested on the amendment that the later enactment effaced.
issues.conclusion: The Court had to proceed as if the effaced amendment had never been introduced, and the High Court judgment founded on it could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory legal fiction must be given full effect and carried to its logical conclusion, including its inevitable consequences. The Court relied on East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and State of Bombay v. Pandurang Vinayak, among other cases. A legislature may alter the law retrospectively and remove the basis of a judgment, but may not simply exercise judicial power by reversing a judgment while leaving its legal basis unchanged. The Court relied on Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality and Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., and distinguished Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India.

rule.if: appeal_against_judgment and judgment_depends_on_prior_amendment and later_law_retroactively_deems_amendment_never_made and later_law_changes_legal_basis

predicates.appeal_against_judgment: A party has appealed a judgment that remains under review.
predicates.judgment_depends_on_prior_amendment: The judgment rests on an earlier statutory amendment.
predicates.later_law_retroactively_deems_amendment_: The legislature later enacted a law that retrospectively treats the earlier amendment as never having been made.
predicates.later_law_changes_legal_basis: The later law changes the legal basis on which the judgment was reached, rather than merely directing that the judgment be disregarded.

issues.definition: When a pending appeal concerns a judgment founded on an amendment that a later law retrospectively treats as never made, and that law changes the judgment’s legal basis, the court applies the altered law and treats the judgment’s basis as removed.

issues.legal_issue: A surplus-land notification issued before a retrospective enactment remains effective where that enactment deems the notification to vest the land from its publication date.
material_facts: A notification declaring the respondent’s excess land surplus had been published before the later enactment.
The later enactment retrospectively removed the amendment that had changed the vesting date and expressly addressed notifications already published.
The later enactment deemed the surplus land specified in such a notification to vest from the date of publication.
issues.conclusion: The existing notification was valid and caused the land to vest on its publication date; no fresh notification was required.
issues.legal_principle: The legal effect of a deeming provision must be carried to its logical conclusion. The later enactment expressly preserved the effect of notifications already published and treated vesting as occurring from their publication dates. The Court relied on the principles concerning statutory fictions in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and the authorities on retrospective validating legislation, including Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality.

rule.if: land_ceiling_proceeding and surplus_notification_previously_published and later_law_retroactively_preserves_published_notifications and later_law_deems_vesting_from_publication

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The dispute concerns the determination and acquisition of surplus land under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.surplus_notification_previously_publishe: An authority had published a notification identifying land as surplus before the later enactment took effect.
predicates.later_law_retroactively_preserves_publis: The legislature enacted a retrospective law preserving the effect of notifications already published.
predicates.later_law_deems_vesting_from_publication: The later law treats the land as vesting from the date the notification was published.

issues.definition: In a land-ceiling proceeding, an already published surplus notification causes vesting without a fresh notification when a retrospective law preserves published notifications and deems vesting to occur on publication.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for surplus land is determined by the rate in force on the date the land vests under the applicable notification.
material_facts: The notification declaring the respondent’s land surplus was published after an amendment had reduced the compensation multiple.
The later enactment was held to preserve vesting from the date of that notification, rather than from the earlier date attributed to vesting by the intervening amendment.
The Court therefore treated the land as having vested after the reduced compensation rate had come into force.
issues.conclusion: Compensation was to be calculated using the reduced rate in force on the notification date, rather than the earlier rate.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 18(3) of the principal Act, as restored by the later enactment, vesting occurred on publication of the section 18(1) notification. Section 50 and Schedule III governed compensation, and the amendment to Schedule III reduced the applicable multiple from nine times to two times of net annual income with effect from its commencement. Because vesting occurred after that change, the reduced rate applied.

predicates.surplus_land_compensation_dispute: The dispute concerns the amount payable for land acquired as surplus under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.vesting_occurs_on_notification_date: The land vests in the government on the date its surplus notification is published.
predicates.notification_date_follows_compensation_r: The notification is published after the compensation rate applicable to surplus land has been reduced.

issues.definition: When surplus land vests on publication of a notification issued after a compensation-rate reduction, compensation uses the rate in force at vesting.

issues.legal_issue: A mandamus directing compliance with a judgment does not independently determine the parties’ rights when it merely implements that judgment.
material_facts: A later mandamus directed the authorities to comply with the earlier compensation judgment.
The mandamus did not independently determine any right or liability between the parties.
The earlier judgment was challenged on appeal and was set aside.
issues.conclusion: The mandamus had no independent consequence once the underlying judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: An order that merely directs execution or compliance with an underlying judgment does not independently determine rights or liabilities; its effect depends on the underlying judgment. The Court treated the mandamus as an execution order and held that it could not survive the setting aside of the judgment it implemented.

predicates.execution_mandamus_challenge: A party disputes the effect of a mandamus that directs compliance with an earlier judgment.
predicates.mandamus_only_directs_compliance: The mandamus directs implementation of the earlier judgment but does not independently determine the parties’ rights or liabilities.
predicates.underlying_judgment_is_set_aside: The judgment that the mandamus directs the authorities to implement is set aside.

issues.definition: A mandamus that only directs compliance with a judgment has no independent effect if that judgment is set aside.
